blocks.html: Part 6: Identity protocols in depth · Module 36
Client authentication, PAR and high-assurance OAuth
Last reviewed 2026-10-05 · Jump to reference

Objective. After this module you can name the method an OAuth client uses to authenticate and say what an attacker needs to impersonate the client under it, check a private_key_jwt assertion claim by claim, say which attack pushed authorization requests, rich authorization requests and step-up authentication each stop, recognize the two legacy grants in a design, and read the FAPI 2.0 Security Profile as a list of separate controls, including what none of them decides.

Before you start. This module builds on four others and does not repeat them. Module 4, OAuth basics teaches the grants, PKCE and redirect URIs. Module 5, JWT validation teaches how to check a JWT. Module 7, Sender-constrained tokens: mTLS and DPoP teaches binding a token to a key. Module 8, Workload and agent identity lifecycle teaches what happens to credentials after they are issued. You should know the difference between authentication and authorization, and what an authorization server, a resource server and an access token are.
Lesson 37 of 38Complete the lesson and quick check, then record your progress.
Learn
1. The attack

Running example: ExamplePay is a payment app. A customer of ExampleBank uses it to pay 45.00 EUR to ExampleAir for a booking. ExamplePay is the OAuth client, ExampleBank runs the authorization server and the payments API. All three companies are fictional.

Suppose ExampleBank built everything module 4 teaches: the authorization code grant, PKCE with S256, exact redirect URI matching, a client secret for ExamplePay and a scope called payments:write. That is a correct deployment. Each row below is an attack it does not stop, and each one has its own control. None of the controls does the job of another.

2. Why it works

Each attack rests on one assumption that the basic flow leaves untested:

  • "The grant decides how the client authenticates." It does not. The grant is how a client obtains a token. Client authentication is how the client proves which client it is, and it is chosen separately. RFC 7523 section 1 says client authentication with a JWT is "nothing more than an alternative way for a client to authenticate to the token endpoint and must be used in conjunction with some grant type".
  • "A client that knows the secret is the client." A client secret is a shared secret. The server can check it, so the server holds something that is enough to pass the check, and with client_secret_basic and client_secret_post the secret itself travels in every token request. Anyone who saw it is the client.
  • "The authorization request is the one my client sent." It crossed the front channel as a URL. RFC 9126 section 1 says of such a request: "There is no cryptographic integrity and authenticity protection." Module 4 told you to treat every value in a redirect as published. It is also editable.
  • "A scope says what was approved." A scope is a short label. RFC 9396 section 1 says scopes are not sufficient for requirements such as "please let me transfer an amount of 45 Euros to Merchant A". A token that says payments:write says nothing about which payment.
  • "A valid token means the user was checked properly, just now." A token is valid for as long as its lifetime says. It records nothing about how the user signed in or how long ago, unless the authorization server writes that down and the resource server reads it.
  • "A deployment that passes a security profile is secure." A profile is a list of controls chosen against a stated attacker. It answers the attacks in its list. It does not decide who may do what to which object, which is object-level authorization.
3. The control

The parts below take the controls one at a time, each with the attack it stops. The last two show what a reviewer still meets from before these controls, and one published way of putting the controls together.
Client authentication is a separate choice

A client registers one method, in the token_endpoint_auth_method client metadata field (RFC 7591 section 2). The server lists the methods it accepts in token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported (RFC 8414 section 2). If nothing is registered the default is client_secret_basic, in both documents and in OpenID Connect Core section 9. RFC 6749 section 2.3 adds one rule for every method: "The client MUST NOT use more than one authentication method in each request."

RFC 9700 section 2.5 recommends the second kind, asymmetric cryptography, for client authentication, and gives the reason: "authorization servers do not need to store sensitive symmetric keys, making these methods more robust against leakage of keys". That is the same step module 3, Asymmetric request signing, took from HMAC to signatures, applied to the client instead of the request. Every row but the last needs a confidential client. Module 7 covers the certificate methods' other use, binding a token to a certificate.
A private_key_jwt assertion, claim by claim

The client builds a client assertion, signs it, and sends it as client_assertion with client_assertion_type set to urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer (RFC 7523 section 2.2). These are the claims the lab's client signs in check 5. The jti is random and is not printed.

{
  "iss": "examplepay",                          the client says who issued this: itself
  "sub": "examplepay",                          and who it is about: itself
  "aud": "https://auth.examplebank.example",    the one server it is meant for
  "iat": 1790003600,
  "exp": 1790003660,                            60 seconds later
  "jti": "<random, used once>"
}
The right-hand notes are for this page only. They are not part of the JWT.

1. Find the client, then use its registered key and algorithm. The sub claim is only a lookup key at this point. Take the algorithm from the registration, never from the JWT header. Module 5 explains algorithm confusion, and check 8 of the lab is that attack against this endpoint.
  2. Verify the signature. RFC 7523 section 3 requires the server to reject a JWT with an invalid signature or MAC.
  3. Check iss and sub. For client authentication RFC 7523 section 3 requires sub to be the client_id, and OpenID Connect Core section 9 requires iss to contain it too.
  4. Check aud. RFC 7523 section 3 requires the server to reject a JWT that does not name the server as an intended audience. Which string names it is the ambiguity discussed below.
  5. Check exp. RFC 7523 section 3 requires an exp claim and requires the server to reject one that has passed. It notes that the server may reject one that is unreasonably far in the future. This project's baseline is to set a cap, because the next step stores something until exp.
  6. Check jti, and record it last. A captured assertion is a replay waiting to happen until it expires. Record the jti only after everything above passed, for the reason module 2, HMAC request signing, gave for nonces: a forged request must not be able to fill the record.
  7. On any failure, answer invalid_client. RFC 7523 section 3.2 requires that error code.

Replay and jti: the sources differ. RFC 7523 section 3 says the JWT may contain a jti and the server may track it, and section 6 is plain about it: "The specification does not mandate replay protection for the JWT usage". OpenID Connect Core section 9, which defines the name private_key_jwt, makes jti required and says: "These tokens MUST only be used once, unless conditions for reuse were negotiated between the parties". So a server can follow RFC 7523 and still accept a replay. Ask which behavior a product implements. RFC 7521 section 8.2 explains why the expiry matters to the record: the validity window relieves the server from keeping processed identifiers forever.

The audience ambiguity. The documents do not agree on which string names the server. RFC 7523 section 3 allows the token endpoint URL. OpenID Connect Core section 9 recommends it. RFC 9126 section 2 names the problem, "Due to historical reasons, there is potential ambiguity regarding the appropriate audience value", and resolves it in two halves: the client should use the authorization server's issuer identifier as the audience, and the server must accept its issuer identifier, its token endpoint URL or its PAR endpoint URL. FAPI 2.0 section 5.3.2.1 is narrower: the server accepts only its issuer identifier, sent as a string and not as an array. Why it matters is this lesson's own reasoning: an assertion that more than one server would accept can be taken from one and presented to another. The narrower the accepted audience, the smaller that set. The OAuth 2.1 Internet-Draft (revision 16) points to a further draft for updated audience guidance. This lesson has not read that draft and does not rely on it.
Pushed authorization requests
A pushed authorization request moves the request parameters off the front channel. RFC 9126 defines it:

1. The client posts the parameters to the PAR endpoint over the back channel. The rules for client authentication at the token endpoint apply here as well (section 2). The server must authenticate the client, reject the request if it carries a request_uri, and validate it as it would an authorization request (section 2.1). Section 1 gives the gain: "PAR allows the authorization server to authenticate the client before any user interaction happens."
  2. The server answers 201 with a request_uri and expires_in (section 2.2). The request_uri is defined there as a single-use reference. It must contain a random part that makes it "computationally infeasible to predict or guess a valid value", and it "MUST be bound to the client that posted the authorization request". The lifetime is the server's choice, and the RFC expects it to be relatively short, for example between 5 and 600 seconds.
  3. The browser carries only client_id and request_uri (section 4). There is nothing else on the URL to edit or to read.
  4. The authorization endpoint looks the reference up. An expired request_uri must be rejected. Servers should treat it as one-time use, and the RFC allows them to accept a duplicate caused by the user reloading the page. The client must use a value only once (section 4).
  5. The server can insist. require_pushed_authorization_requests is both server metadata (section 5) and client metadata (section 6), and defaults to false in both. When it applies, the server refuses any authorization request without a request_uri from the PAR endpoint, with invalid_request (section 4). Without that setting an attacker simply does not use PAR.

Section 7 of the RFC lists what can still go wrong with the reference itself:

  • Guessing (7.1). The server must account for the considerations in RFC 9101 section 10.2, clause (d), on entropy. That clause requires a short lifetime and sufficiently large entropy, and gives as general guidance a validity of less than a minute and a random value of 128 bits or more.
  • Open redirection (7.2). PAR lets a server accept a redirect URI that was not registered in advance. The server must accept new redirect URIs in a pushed request only from authenticated clients.
  • Replay (7.3). An attacker could replay a captured request URI, so the server should make request URIs one-time use.
  • Client policy change (7.4). The client's policy can change between the push and the authorization request, so the RFC recommends checking the request against the client policy again at the authorization endpoint.
  • Swapping (7.5). An attacker could substitute a request URI from one request into another. Clients should use PKCE, a unique state or the OpenID Connect nonce to prevent it.

JAR in brief. RFC 9101 defines the other way to protect the request: the client signs the parameters into a request object, a JWT, and sends it in the request parameter or by reference in request_uri. PAR borrows that request_uri parameter. RFC 9126 section 1 says PAR "complements JAR", and section 3 allows a client to push a signed request object, which is the choice for a client that needs to prove afterwards what it asked for. FAPI 2.0 replaced the request object of FAPI 1.0 with PAR, and its section 5.5 gives the reason as "integrity protection and compatibility improvements for authorization requests".
Rich authorization requests
RFC 9396 adds one parameter, authorization_details, which carries authorization details: a JSON array of objects. This is the request the lab's client pushes:

[{
  "type": "payment_initiation",
  "actions": ["initiate", "status"],
  "locations": ["https://api.examplebank.example/payments"],
  "instructedAmount": {"currency": "EUR", "amount": "45.00"},
  "creditorName": "ExampleAir",
  "creditorAccount": "acct-exampleair"
}]

• type is the only required field, and it "determines the allowable contents of the object that contains it" (section 2). The API defines its types. The authorization server controls how each is interpreted (section 2.1).
  • Five common fields are offered for reuse and none is mandatory: locations, actions, datatypes, identifier and privileges (section 2.2). instructedAmount, creditorName and creditorAccount above belong to this API's type, as in the RFC's own payment example.
  • The server refuses what the type does not allow. Section 5 requires it to answer invalid_authorization_details for an unknown type, an unknown field, a field of the wrong type, an invalid value or a missing required field.
  • The token response says what was granted. Section 7 requires the server to return the authorization_details "as granted by the resource owner and assigned to the respective access token". They may differ from what was asked (section 7.1), and a note in section 3 says the user may grant a subset. This lesson's advice is that the client compares the two.
  • The resource server is told. Section 9 requires the authorization server to make the data available to the resource server. For a JWT access token it recommends a top-level claim (9.1). In an introspection response, if included, it must be the top-level member authorization_details (9.2).
  • Scope still works alongside. If both are present the server must process them together and must show the user the merged set (section 3.1).

What the resource server must still do. Everything. Section 1 of the RFC says the authorization server and the resource server "will together enforce this consent". The object in the token is data. If the payments API checks that a payment_initiation object is present and does not compare its fields with the payment in front of it, the token is as broad as the scope was. Check 44 of the lab is that API. How to compare is the API's own definition: section 6.1 says "there is no standardized mechanism to compare two arbitrary authorization detail requests".

The specification's own security considerations (section 12): the parameter travels through the user agent, so the user can modify it, and "clients MUST protect authorization_details against tampering and swapping" where integrity is a concern, with a signed request object or with PAR. String comparisons follow RFC 8259 with no further normalization. The server must sanitize the data to prevent injection. Section 13 adds that personal data in the details must be kept from leaking, for example through referrer headers. In a payment both concerns are real. Section 3 says implementers may consider PAR for exactly this, and Part C of the lab pushes every request that carries details.

Two connections. Module 23, Agent authority and approvals, teaches that an approval must bind the exact parameters that will execute. authorization_details is where OAuth carries those parameters from the consent screen to the API. And RAR does not replace server-side authorization: it narrows what a token may do, and the API still decides whose objects the caller may touch, which is module 9, Object-level authorization.
Step-up authentication
Step-up authentication lets a resource server refuse one request because of how, or how long ago, the user authenticated. RFC 9470 defines it in four moves:

1. The resource server reads two facts about the token: auth_time, when the user authenticated, and acr, an authentication context class reference that names how. They come from the claims of a JWT access token (section 6.1) or from the introspection response (section 6.2). Section 6.1 notes that the values "will not change in the event of access token renewals": a refreshed token is not a fresher authentication.
  2. If they do not meet its policy, it challenges. The error code is insufficient_user_authentication. Two parameters say what would be enough: acr_values, a space-separated list in order of preference, and max_age, the allowed number of seconds since the last active authentication. Both may appear in one challenge (section 3).
  3. The client starts a new authorization request carrying those values as the acr_values and max_age request parameters that OpenID Connect Core section 3.1.2.1 defines (section 4, which says the client should do this). The client does not look inside the access token to decide: section 2 says "a client must not attempt to inspect the content of the access token".
  4. The authorization server authenticates the user again and issues a new token whose acr and auth_time reflect it. Section 5 says the server should treat the requested acr as necessary: if it cannot be met, the request fails with unmet_authentication_requirements. That stops a client looping on tokens the API has already refused.

An acr value is only a string. OpenID Connect Core section 2 says: "Parties using this claim will need to agree upon the meanings of the values used". The resource server trusts the authorization server's statement that a second factor was used. RFC 9470 section 9 adds two cautions. The challenge can tell an attacker which users or resources are treated as high value. And a resource server may send the challenge without first validating the token, but doing so leaks its requirements to a caller who has not shown it can obtain a token. The lab validates first.

This is not the step-up in module 20. Module 20, MCP server authorization teaches the MCP specification's "Step-Up Authorization Flow". The words are similar and the thing is different:

Legacy flows a reviewer will meet
Module 4 gives these one table row. Here is the fuller account, because both still appear in designs and in server defaults.

FAPI 2.0: one published composition

The FAPI 2.0 Security Profile is an OpenID Foundation Final Specification (22 February 2025). It selects from the controls above and from modules 4 and 7, and makes them mandatory together. Its keywords are "shall", "should" and "may".

The attacker model, as far as this lesson can state it. The profile says it "has been proved by formal analysis to meet the stated attacker model" (section 1), and that it aims to follow the recommendations in RFC 9700 (section 5.1.1). The attacker model is a separate document, the FAPI 2.0 Attacker Model, which this lesson has not read, so it is not summarized here. What this lesson can report is a different list, the attacker model of RFC 9700 itself (section 3). It is not the FAPI one. It describes five kinds of attacker: a web attacker who runs their own clients, servers and pages (A1), a network attacker who controls the network outside what cryptography such as TLS protects (A2), and attackers who can read the authorization response (A3), read the authorization request (A4), or acquire an access token (A5). The profile's own security considerations mention an attacker who can intercept an authorization request and one who can obtain DPoP proofs, and call them A3 and A5 in its own model's numbering (sections 6.4 and 6.2). In RFC 9700 the attacker who reads the authorization request is A4, not A3, so the two lists number their attackers differently. Do not carry one over to the other. The profile also says what it leaves out: only confidential clients are in scope, because the working group "is not currently aware of any mechanisms that would allow public clients to be secured to the same degree" (section 5.1.1).

Three things about that list. First, the profile does not require RAR. A note in section 5.3.2.2 recommends it "when the scope parameter is not expressive enough". It does not mention RFC 9470 at all. A deployment can meet the profile with a coarse scope and no step-up, so Part E of the lab adds both on its own account. Second, a few requirements cut against habit: the server shall not use refresh token rotation except in extraordinary circumstances (5.3.2.1). Its note gives the reason: rotation brings no security benefit with confidential clients and sender-constrained tokens, and it causes operational problems. Third, the profile says what it does not solve. Section 6.5 describes a browser-swapping attack and says "there is no way to completely prevent this attack if the authorization response leaks to an attacker in any redirect-based protocol". Section 6.2 notes that DPoP does not sign the request body. Section 5.1.2 forbids a derived profile from removing mandatory behaviors, because doing so "is likely to invalidate the formal security analysis".

The teaching point. High assurance is a composition: each control answers one named attack by one kind of attacker, and the list is only as good as the attacker model behind it. An API can have every control above in place and still return another customer's payment to a correctly authenticated caller. The profile has one clause that touches this: the resource server shall verify that the authorization the token represents is sufficient for the requested resource access (5.3.4). It does not say how, and no other control in the list looks at which object was asked for. Deciding whose object it is stays the API's own code. That is module 9, and it is check 70 of the lab.

5. What it proves, and what it doesn't

Proves, control by control: private_key_jwt proves the caller can use the private key that matches the public key registered for this client, for this server, within the assertion's short lifetime, and once if the server tracks jti. PAR proves the parameters the server acted on are the ones an authenticated client sent it directly. authorization_details on a token prove which specific access the authorization server recorded as granted. acr and auth_time are the authorization server's statement of how and when the user authenticated. A deployment that meets FAPI 2.0 has all of the controls in the table in section 3, analyzed together against a stated attacker.

Doesn't prove who may do what to which object. Every control here is about the client, the request, the token or the user's authentication. None of them looks at whether the object named in the API call belongs to the caller. That decision is made in the API, per object and per operation (modules 9 and 10, Property and function authorization).

Doesn't prove the user understood what they approved. RAR makes the consent screen able to show the real payee and amount. It cannot make anyone read it. In check 21 of the lab the user is shown a request that was edited in the browser, and approves it. FAPI 2.0 section 7 lists "Insufficient understanding of the end-user granting access to data" among its privacy threats. Module 23 covers the same limit for agent approvals.

Doesn't prove anything about where the client keeps its private key. Asymmetric client authentication moves the target from the server's table to the client's key. If that key sits in a repository or an environment variable, anyone who reads it is the client, with a credential that looks stronger on paper. Who owns that key, when it rotates and how it is withdrawn is module 8.

Doesn't make a token single use. Nothing in RFC 9396 limits how many times a token may be used. Measured on a call the lab does not make: the token from check 38 pays 45.00 EUR to ExampleAir a second time and gets 201 again. One approved payment being executed once is a rule for the API to enforce, and it is module 11, Business flows and idempotency.

Step-up is not sign-in. RFC 9470 section 9 says: "This document MUST NOT be used to position OAuth as an authentication protocol." The resource server learns how the authorization server authenticated the user. The client learns nothing about who the user is, and must not treat the new access token as a login. Module 4 makes the same point about access tokens in general.
6. Prove it

A working deployment must refuse every one of these. If any is accepted, the control it belongs to is broken:

  • A client registered for private_key_jwt presenting a client secret, or presenting two methods in one request.
  • An assertion signed with any key other than the registered one, or with an algorithm other than the registered one, including an HMAC keyed with the client's public key.
  • An assertion whose aud names another server. If your policy is issuer-only, one whose aud is the token endpoint URL.
  • An assertion presented at or after its exp, one whose exp is further away than your cap, and the same assertion presented twice.
  • With PAR required: an authorization request that carries its parameters on the URL.
  • A request_uri used a second time, used after expires_in, made up, or presented with a different client_id. After the last of these, the rightful client can still use it.
  • A pushed request with no client authentication, and one that itself contains a request_uri.
  • Parameters added to the authorization URL next to a request_uri: they must have no effect.
  • An authorization_details object with an unknown type, an unknown field or a missing field, and a known type the client is not registered to use.
  • At the API: a payment whose payee, amount or currency differs from the granted object in any way.
  • At the API: a consequential request with a token whose auth_time is older than the policy or whose acr is weaker. The refusal names insufficient_user_authentication and says what is required. An invalid token on the same endpoint gets invalid_token and no policy.
  • response_type=token, grant_type=password and code_challenge_method=plain.
  • In the client: an authorization response whose iss is not the issuer the request was sent to.
  • A bound token presented without the key it is bound to.
  • And, with every one of the above in place: a request for an object that belongs to another customer.

8. Check your understanding

A design says "the service uses the client credentials grant, so it authenticates with a client secret". What is wrong with the sentence?

It treats two choices as one. The client credentials grant is how the client obtains a token. The client authentication method is how it proves which client it is, and any method can be used with that grant, including private_key_jwt and mutual TLS. Ask which method is registered, and what an attacker would need in order to use it.

A server validates client assertions exactly as RFC 7523 section 3 requires. An attacker copies one assertion from a log 20 seconds after it was made. What happens?

It may well be accepted. RFC 7523 requires the signature, iss, sub, aud and exp checks, and the copy passes all of them until it expires. Tracking jti is optional in that RFC. OpenID Connect Core section 9 requires single use. Check 11 of the lab is the first server and check 10 is the second.

An API returns 401 with error="insufficient_user_authentication" and max_age="300". The client refreshes its access token and retries. Does that work?

No. RFC 9470 section 6.1 says auth_time and acr are set when the user authenticates and do not change when a token is renewed. The client has to send the user through a new authorization request that carries max_age=300, so that the authorization server authenticates the user again.

A vendor says its payments API is FAPI 2.0 certified. Name two things that statement does not tell you.

Whether the API checks that the object in a request belongs to the caller, and whether a payment is limited to the payee and amount the user approved. The profile only recommends RAR. For the first it has one general clause (section 5.3.4: the resource server shall verify that the authorization the token represents is sufficient for the request), and it defines no per-object rule, so that check is the API's own code. It also says nothing about how each client stores its private key, or whether a user understood the consent screen.

attrs.data-correct-feedback: Correct. The scope says the token may make payments. Only authorization_details that name the payee and the amount, enforced field by field at the API, limit which payment.
attrs.data-incorrect-feedback: Not quite. Each of the other controls is real and stops a different attack: who the client is, whether the request was edited, or how recently the user signed in. None of them limits which payment a token with payments:write may make.

Exercises

Change one thing and predict the output

Each exercise edits one place in labs/advanced_oauth_lab.py and asks what the run prints. The answers are the real output of each variant, not a reading of the code. The lab compares every result with the one it expects, so each of these edits makes it exit 1 and list what differed. All four need the cryptography package, as the lab does.

1. The server stops checking the assertion's audience

In AuthorizationServer._authenticate_assertion, delete the two lines that call self._audience_ok and return invalid_client: audience. Everything else, including the signature check, stays.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 12 does flip, and it is not alone. The issuer-only server in check 17 refuses its assertion for one reason, the audience, and that reason is the code this edit deletes.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures: checks 12 and 17 both go from invalid_client: audience to authenticated. Check 12 is an assertion ExamplePay signed for https://auth.other.example. Its signature is genuine, so nothing else refuses it. Any server that receives a client's assertion can now present it here, which is what check aoa-02 in the Reference layer asks you to rule out.
  • Check 16 already printed authenticated and still does. An edit that removes a refusal cannot change a check that was an acceptance.
  • The signature proves who made the assertion. It does not prove which server it was made for. Those are different claims, and aud is the only one that carries the second.

2. The request_uri is no longer bound to the client

In AuthorizationServer.authorize, delete the two lines that compare entry["client_id"] with the client making the request and return request_uri belongs to another client. The expiry and one-time-use checks stay.

What does the run print differently?

Every option, and why
  • Check 30 is right. Check 31 is the same request_uri, presented next by ExamplePay, and the one-time-use rule is still in force. The other client has just used it.
  • The server finds pushed requests by the request_uri alone. The value exists, so the lookup succeeds. The binding was a separate comparison, and it is the one that was deleted.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures. Check 30 goes from invalid_request: request_uri belongs to another client to code issued: a second client has started an authorization on ExamplePay's pushed request. Check 31 goes from code issued to invalid_request: request_uri already used: ExamplePay is locked out of its own request. RFC 9126 section 2.2 requires the binding, and check aoa-04 in the Reference layer tests for it.
  • Check 29 is a made-up value, which is still unknown to the server. It prints the same as before.

3. The API stops comparing the amount

In PaymentsAPI._covers, delete the line that compares d["instructedAmount"].get("amount") with body["amount"]. The creditor account and the currency are still compared.

Which checks change?

Every option, and why
  • Check 42 pays a different account, and the account is still compared. It still prints 403 Bearer error="insufficient_scope".
  • Correct. Exit 1, one failure: check 43 goes from 403 Bearer error="insufficient_scope" to 201 paid 450.00 EUR to acct-exampleair. The user approved 45.00 and the token still says 45.00. The API paid ten times that to the right payee, because one field of the granted object was no longer read. Check aoa-05 in the Reference layer says every field for this reason.
  • Check 44 runs against the API that checks only the type. It never compared the amount, so it already printed 201 and prints the same.
  • The authorization server validated the request and recorded 45.00. It is not present when the token is used. Only the resource server sees the payment that is actually submitted.

4. The step-up policy joins its two conditions with "and"

In PaymentsAPI.handle, the policy line reads if info["acr"] != ACR_MFA or age > PAYMENT_MAX_AGE:. Change or to and.

Which of the three challenged payments, checks 52, 56 and 57, still get a challenge?

Every option, and why
  • With and, a token is challenged only when it is both weak and old. Two of the three fail on one count only.
  • Check 56 is a second-factor sign-in from 30 minutes ago. Its acr is the required one, so the first half of the condition is false and the whole condition is false.
  • Correct. Exit 1, two failures: checks 56 and 57 both go from the insufficient_user_authentication challenge to 201 paid 45.00 EUR to acct-exampleair. Check 52, a password sign-in two hours old, fails on both counts and is still challenged. A test with only that one token would pass on the broken policy, which is why check aoa-07 in the Reference layer asks for a token that is old but strong and one that is fresh but weak.
  • Check 52 is weak and old, so even the loosened condition is true for it.

Reference
Controls
Standard backed by a cited specification. Baseline this project's default, with reasoning above. Option valid depending on the threat model.

• StandardRFC 9700 section 2.5 recommends asymmetric cryptography for client authentication, such as mutual TLS (RFC 8705) or signed JWTs (private_key_jwt), and says authorization servers should enforce client authentication where issuing and protecting client credentials is feasible.
  • StandardThe client must not use more than one authentication method in a request. RFC 6749 section 2.3. The server must not rely on public client authentication to identify the client. Same section.
  • StandardA JWT used for client authentication must contain iss, sub equal to the client_id, an aud that identifies the authorization server, and exp, and must be signed or carry a MAC. The server must reject one with an invalid signature or MAC, one that does not name it as audience, and one that has expired. RFC 7523 section 3. Failures are reported as invalid_client. RFC 7523 section 3.2.
  • StandardRFC 7523 section 3 allows, and does not require, a jti claim and replay tracking. OpenID Connect Core 1.0 incorporating errata set 2, section 9, requires jti for private_key_jwt and client_secret_jwt and requires that the assertion be used only once unless the parties negotiated otherwise.
  • StandardFor JWT client authentication the client should use the authorization server's issuer identifier as the audience, and the server must accept its issuer identifier, its token endpoint URL or its PAR endpoint URL. RFC 9126 section 2.
  • StandardThe PAR endpoint must authenticate the client as the token endpoint does, must reject a pushed request that contains request_uri, and must validate the request as it would an authorization request. RFC 9126 section 2.1.
  • StandardThe request_uri must contain a part generated with a cryptographically strong pseudorandom algorithm so that guessing a valid value is computationally infeasible, and must be bound to the client that posted the request. RFC 9126 section 2.2.
  • StandardAn expired request_uri must be rejected. The server should treat request_uri values as one-time use and may allow a duplicate caused by a reload. The client must use a value only once. RFC 9126 section 4.
  • StandardServer policy may make PAR the only way to pass authorization request data, globally or per client, signalled by require_pushed_authorization_requests. The server then refuses other authorization requests with invalid_request. RFC 9126 sections 4, 5 and 6.
  • StandardThe server must accept new redirect URIs in a pushed request only from authenticated clients. RFC 9126 section 7.2. Clients should use PKCE, a unique state or the OpenID Connect nonce against request URI swapping. RFC 9126 section 7.5.
  • StandardEach authorization_details object requires a type. The server must refuse an unknown type, unknown fields, fields of the wrong type, invalid values and missing required fields, with invalid_authorization_details. RFC 9396 sections 2 and 5.
  • StandardThe token response must return the authorization_details as granted, and the authorization server must make them available to the resource server. RFC 9396 sections 7 and 9.
  • StandardIf the integrity of authorization_details is a concern, clients must protect them against tampering and swapping, with a signed request object or with PAR. The server must sanitize the data to prevent injection. RFC 9396 section 12.
  • StandardA resource server signals that the authentication behind a token is not sufficient with the error code insufficient_user_authentication, and may state the requirement with acr_values, max_age or both. RFC 9470 section 3. The client should use those values in a new authorization request. RFC 9470 section 4.
  • StandardThe authorization server should treat a requested acr as necessary when issuing the access token, and fail the request if it cannot be met. RFC 9470 section 5. RFC 9470 must not be used to position OAuth as an authentication protocol. RFC 9470 section 9.
  • StandardThe resource owner password credentials grant must not be used. RFC 9700 section 2.4. Clients should not use the implicit grant or other response types that return an access token in the authorization response, unless access token injection is prevented and the leakage vectors that section names are mitigated. RFC 9700 section 2.1.2.
  • StandardA client that can interact with more than one authorization server is required to have a defense against mix-up attacks, and should use the iss parameter of RFC 9207 or an equivalent issuer value in the response. RFC 9700 section 2.1. A client that supports RFC 9207 must compare iss with the issuer of the server the request was sent to and reject a mismatch. RFC 9207 section 2.4.
  • StandardUnder the FAPI 2.0 Security Profile, authorization servers shall authenticate clients with mutual TLS or private_key_jwt, shall reject authorization requests sent without PAR, shall require PKCE with S256, shall return iss, shall issue only sender-constrained access tokens, and shall reject the password grant. FAPI 2.0 Security Profile sections 5.3.2.1 and 5.3.2.2. Resource servers shall verify the token and that the authorization it represents is sufficient. Section 5.3.4.
  • BaselineRegister private_key_jwt for every confidential client. Accept one audience, the issuer identifier. Cap the assertion lifetime and record each jti until exp, after the signature and claims have passed.
  • BaselineTake the assertion's algorithm and key from the client's registration, never from the JWT header.
  • BaselineRequire PAR for every client whose request parameters matter. Use only what was pushed, and ignore anything else on the authorization URL.
  • BaselinePut anything with an amount, a payee or a named object in authorization_details. At the API, compare every field of the granted object with the request. Build the consent text from the same object.
  • BaselineValidate the token before applying the step-up policy, so that an invalid token is not told what the policy is.
  • BaselineTreat a profile claim as a list to verify row by row, and test object-level authorization separately.

Review checklist items
These are collected into the site checklist.

  • Client assertions are checked for signature, issuer, subject, one audience, expiry and single use Test an assertion made for another server, an expired one, one with a far exp, and the same one twice. The algorithm comes from the registration.
  • Pushed authorization requests are required, not just supported require_pushed_authorization_requests is set for the server or the client, and an authorization request with parameters on the URL is refused.
  • A request_uri is single use, short lived, unguessable and bound to its client Test a second use, a use after expires_in, a made-up value and a use with another client_id. Confirm the rightful client can still use it after the last one.
  • Transaction parameters are in authorization_details and the API enforces every field Test a payment that differs from the granted object in payee, in amount and in currency, one at a time. Each must be refused.
  • The authorization server refuses details it does not define or the client may not use Unknown types, unknown fields and missing fields get invalid_authorization_details. The client compares the token response with what it asked for.
  • Consequential operations check acr and auth_time and challenge when either falls short Test a token that is old but strong and one that is fresh but weak. Both get insufficient_user_authentication with the required acr_values and max_age.
  • No implicit or password grant is reachable, including by default Read grant_types_supported and each client's grant_types and response_types. Metadata that omits grant_types_supported defaults to including implicit.
  • Clients check the iss parameter of the authorization response A response whose iss is not the issuer the request went to is dropped before the code is redeemed. RFC 9700 requires a mix-up defense of any client that uses more than one authorization server.
  • A profile claim is not accepted as evidence of authorization With every control above in place, request an object that belongs to another customer. No control in the profile makes that check for the API. The API must refuse.

intro_prose:
Objective. After this module you can name the method an OAuth client uses to authenticate and say what an attacker needs to impersonate the client under it, check a private_key_jwt assertion claim by claim, say which attack pushed authorization requests, rich authorization requests and step-up authentication each stop, recognize the two legacy grants in a design, and read the FAPI 2.0 Security Profile as a list of separate controls, including what none of them decides.

Before you start. This module builds on four others and does not repeat them. Module 4, OAuth basics teaches the grants, PKCE and redirect URIs. Module 5, JWT validation teaches how to check a JWT. Module 7, Sender-constrained tokens: mTLS and DPoP teaches binding a token to a key. Module 8, Workload and agent identity lifecycle teaches what happens to credentials after they are issued. You should know the difference between authentication and authorization, and what an authorization server, a resource server and an access token are.

sections.heading: 1. The attack
sections.html:
Running example: ExamplePay is a payment app. A customer of ExampleBank uses it to pay 45.00 EUR to ExampleAir for a booking. ExamplePay is the OAuth client, ExampleBank runs the authorization server and the payments API. All three companies are fictional.

Suppose ExampleBank built everything module 4 teaches: the authorization code grant, PKCE with S256, exact redirect URI matching, a client secret for ExamplePay and a scope called payments:write. That is a correct deployment. Each row below is an attack it does not stop, and each one has its own control. None of the controls does the job of another.

The attackerCode grant with PKCE, a client secret and a scopeWith the added controlThe control
Reads ExamplePay's client secret in a proxy log or in the server's client table, then authenticates as ExamplePayWorksBlocked: the server holds a public key, and no secret travelsprivate_key_jwt or mutual TLS client authentication
Edits the authorization request in the browser before it reaches the serverWorks: the server acts on what arrivedBlocked: the browser carries only a referencePushed authorization requests (PAR)
Uses a token with payments:write to pay a different account a different amountWorksBlocked: the token names one payee and one amount, and the API enforces bothRich authorization requests (RAR)
Makes a payment on a session that signed in with a password two hours agoWorksChallenged: the API asks for a fresh, stronger authenticationStep-up authentication
Copies the access token and uses it from another machineWorksBlockedA sender-constrained token (module 7)
Is a real, correctly authenticated customer and asks for another customer's paymentWorksWorksNone of the above. An ownership check (module 9, Object-level authorization)

The last row stays red whichever of these controls you add. Section 5 comes back to it, and Part E of the lab runs it.

sections.heading: 2. Why it works
sections.html:
Each attack rests on one assumption that the basic flow leaves untested:

  • "The grant decides how the client authenticates." It does not. The grant is how a client obtains a token. Client authentication is how the client proves which client it is, and it is chosen separately. RFC 7523 section 1 says client authentication with a JWT is "nothing more than an alternative way for a client to authenticate to the token endpoint and must be used in conjunction with some grant type".
  • "A client that knows the secret is the client." A client secret is a shared secret. The server can check it, so the server holds something that is enough to pass the check, and with client_secret_basic and client_secret_post the secret itself travels in every token request. Anyone who saw it is the client.
  • "The authorization request is the one my client sent." It crossed the front channel as a URL. RFC 9126 section 1 says of such a request: "There is no cryptographic integrity and authenticity protection." Module 4 told you to treat every value in a redirect as published. It is also editable.
  • "A scope says what was approved." A scope is a short label. RFC 9396 section 1 says scopes are not sufficient for requirements such as "please let me transfer an amount of 45 Euros to Merchant A". A token that says payments:write says nothing about which payment.
  • "A valid token means the user was checked properly, just now." A token is valid for as long as its lifetime says. It records nothing about how the user signed in or how long ago, unless the authorization server writes that down and the resource server reads it.
  • "A deployment that passes a security profile is secure." A profile is a list of controls chosen against a stated attacker. It answers the attacks in its list. It does not decide who may do what to which object, which is object-level authorization.

sections.heading: 3. The control
sections.html:
The parts below take the controls one at a time, each with the attack it stops. The last two show what a reviewer still meets from before these controls, and one published way of putting the controls together.

Client authentication is a separate choice

A client registers one method, in the token_endpoint_auth_method client metadata field (RFC 7591 section 2). The server lists the methods it accepts in token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported (RFC 8414 section 2). If nothing is registered the default is client_secret_basic, in both documents and in OpenID Connect Core section 9. RFC 6749 section 2.3 adds one rule for every method: "The client MUST NOT use more than one authentication method in each request."

MethodWhere the name is definedWhat the client sendsWhat the server storesWhat an attacker needs
client_secret_basicRFC 7591 section 2 and OpenID Connect Core section 9, for the mechanism in RFC 6749 section 2.3.1The secret itself, in an HTTP Basic header, on every requestThe secret, or a hash of itThe secret, from any place it has been: the client's configuration, a log or proxy that saw the header, or the server's table if it is not hashed
client_secret_postThe same three documentsThe secret itself, in the request body. RFC 6749 section 2.3.1 says this form is not recommended and should be limited to clients that cannot use the Basic schemeAs aboveAs above
client_secret_jwtOpenID Connect Core section 9, using RFC 7523A JWT carrying an HMAC keyed with the secret. The secret does not travelThe secret itself. It cannot be a hash, because the server needs the key to recompute the HMACThe secret, from the client or from the server's table
private_key_jwtOpenID Connect Core section 9, using RFC 7523A JWT signed with the client's private keyA public keyThe client's private key. Or one captured assertion, until it expires, if the server does not track jti
tls_client_authRFC 8705 section 2.1.1A client certificate in the TLS handshake. The server validates the chain and compares one registered subject nameThe expected subject and the trusted certificate authoritiesThe private key of a certificate with that subject. This lesson's own addition: so the certificate authorities the server trusts are part of what you review
self_signed_tls_client_authRFC 8705 section 2.2.1A client certificate in the TLS handshake. The chain is not validated. The certificate must be one the client registeredThe client's certificates, or a jwks_uri to fetch them fromThe private key of a registered certificate. This lesson's own addition: or control of what the jwks_uri serves
noneRFC 7591 section 2Nothing. The client is a public clientNothingNothing. RFC 6749 section 2.3 says the server "MUST NOT rely on public client authentication for the purpose of identifying the client". PKCE protects the code, not the client's identity

The first three rows are one kind of credential and the next three are another. RFC 9700 section 2.5 recommends the second kind, asymmetric cryptography, for client authentication, and gives the reason: "authorization servers do not need to store sensitive symmetric keys, making these methods more robust against leakage of keys". That is the same step module 3, Asymmetric request signing, took from HMAC to signatures, applied to the client instead of the request. Every row but the last needs a confidential client. Module 7 covers the certificate methods' other use, binding a token to a certificate.

A private_key_jwt assertion, claim by claim

The client builds a client assertion, signs it, and sends it as client_assertion with client_assertion_type set to urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer (RFC 7523 section 2.2). These are the claims the lab's client signs in check 5. The jti is random and is not printed.

{
  "iss": "examplepay",                          the client says who issued this: itself
  "sub": "examplepay",                          and who it is about: itself
  "aud": "https://auth.examplebank.example",    the one server it is meant for
  "iat": 1790003600,
  "exp": 1790003660,                            60 seconds later
  "jti": "<random, used once>"
}

The right-hand notes are for this page only. They are not part of the JWT.

  1. Find the client, then use its registered key and algorithm. The sub claim is only a lookup key at this point. Take the algorithm from the registration, never from the JWT header. Module 5 explains algorithm confusion, and check 8 of the lab is that attack against this endpoint.
  2. Verify the signature. RFC 7523 section 3 requires the server to reject a JWT with an invalid signature or MAC.
  3. Check iss and sub. For client authentication RFC 7523 section 3 requires sub to be the client_id, and OpenID Connect Core section 9 requires iss to contain it too.
  4. Check aud. RFC 7523 section 3 requires the server to reject a JWT that does not name the server as an intended audience. Which string names it is the ambiguity discussed below.
  5. Check exp. RFC 7523 section 3 requires an exp claim and requires the server to reject one that has passed. It notes that the server may reject one that is unreasonably far in the future. This project's baseline is to set a cap, because the next step stores something until exp.
  6. Check jti, and record it last. A captured assertion is a replay waiting to happen until it expires. Record the jti only after everything above passed, for the reason module 2, HMAC request signing, gave for nonces: a forged request must not be able to fill the record.
  7. On any failure, answer invalid_client. RFC 7523 section 3.2 requires that error code.

Replay and jti: the sources differ. RFC 7523 section 3 says the JWT may contain a jti and the server may track it, and section 6 is plain about it: "The specification does not mandate replay protection for the JWT usage". OpenID Connect Core section 9, which defines the name private_key_jwt, makes jti required and says: "These tokens MUST only be used once, unless conditions for reuse were negotiated between the parties". So a server can follow RFC 7523 and still accept a replay. Ask which behavior a product implements. RFC 7521 section 8.2 explains why the expiry matters to the record: the validity window relieves the server from keeping processed identifiers forever.

The audience ambiguity. The documents do not agree on which string names the server. RFC 7523 section 3 allows the token endpoint URL. OpenID Connect Core section 9 recommends it. RFC 9126 section 2 names the problem, "Due to historical reasons, there is potential ambiguity regarding the appropriate audience value", and resolves it in two halves: the client should use the authorization server's issuer identifier as the audience, and the server must accept its issuer identifier, its token endpoint URL or its PAR endpoint URL. FAPI 2.0 section 5.3.2.1 is narrower: the server accepts only its issuer identifier, sent as a string and not as an array. Why it matters is this lesson's own reasoning: an assertion that more than one server would accept can be taken from one and presented to another. The narrower the accepted audience, the smaller that set. The OAuth 2.1 Internet-Draft (revision 16) points to a further draft for updated audience guidance. This lesson has not read that draft and does not rely on it.

Pushed authorization requests

A pushed authorization request moves the request parameters off the front channel. RFC 9126 defines it:

  1. The client posts the parameters to the PAR endpoint over the back channel. The rules for client authentication at the token endpoint apply here as well (section 2). The server must authenticate the client, reject the request if it carries a request_uri, and validate it as it would an authorization request (section 2.1). Section 1 gives the gain: "PAR allows the authorization server to authenticate the client before any user interaction happens."
  2. The server answers 201 with a request_uri and expires_in (section 2.2). The request_uri is defined there as a single-use reference. It must contain a random part that makes it "computationally infeasible to predict or guess a valid value", and it "MUST be bound to the client that posted the authorization request". The lifetime is the server's choice, and the RFC expects it to be relatively short, for example between 5 and 600 seconds.
  3. The browser carries only client_id and request_uri (section 4). There is nothing else on the URL to edit or to read.
  4. The authorization endpoint looks the reference up. An expired request_uri must be rejected. Servers should treat it as one-time use, and the RFC allows them to accept a duplicate caused by the user reloading the page. The client must use a value only once (section 4).
  5. The server can insist. require_pushed_authorization_requests is both server metadata (section 5) and client metadata (section 6), and defaults to false in both. When it applies, the server refuses any authorization request without a request_uri from the PAR endpoint, with invalid_request (section 4). Without that setting an attacker simply does not use PAR.

Section 7 of the RFC lists what can still go wrong with the reference itself:

  • Guessing (7.1). The server must account for the considerations in RFC 9101 section 10.2, clause (d), on entropy. That clause requires a short lifetime and sufficiently large entropy, and gives as general guidance a validity of less than a minute and a random value of 128 bits or more.
  • Open redirection (7.2). PAR lets a server accept a redirect URI that was not registered in advance. The server must accept new redirect URIs in a pushed request only from authenticated clients.
  • Replay (7.3). An attacker could replay a captured request URI, so the server should make request URIs one-time use.
  • Client policy change (7.4). The client's policy can change between the push and the authorization request, so the RFC recommends checking the request against the client policy again at the authorization endpoint.
  • Swapping (7.5). An attacker could substitute a request URI from one request into another. Clients should use PKCE, a unique state or the OpenID Connect nonce to prevent it.

JAR in brief. RFC 9101 defines the other way to protect the request: the client signs the parameters into a request object, a JWT, and sends it in the request parameter or by reference in request_uri. PAR borrows that request_uri parameter. RFC 9126 section 1 says PAR "complements JAR", and section 3 allows a client to push a signed request object, which is the choice for a client that needs to prove afterwards what it asked for. FAPI 2.0 replaced the request object of FAPI 1.0 with PAR, and its section 5.5 gives the reason as "integrity protection and compatibility improvements for authorization requests".

Rich authorization requests

RFC 9396 adds one parameter, authorization_details, which carries authorization details: a JSON array of objects. This is the request the lab's client pushes:

[{
  "type": "payment_initiation",
  "actions": ["initiate", "status"],
  "locations": ["https://api.examplebank.example/payments"],
  "instructedAmount": {"currency": "EUR", "amount": "45.00"},
  "creditorName": "ExampleAir",
  "creditorAccount": "acct-exampleair"
}]
  • type is the only required field, and it "determines the allowable contents of the object that contains it" (section 2). The API defines its types. The authorization server controls how each is interpreted (section 2.1).
  • Five common fields are offered for reuse and none is mandatory: locations, actions, datatypes, identifier and privileges (section 2.2). instructedAmount, creditorName and creditorAccount above belong to this API's type, as in the RFC's own payment example.
  • The server refuses what the type does not allow. Section 5 requires it to answer invalid_authorization_details for an unknown type, an unknown field, a field of the wrong type, an invalid value or a missing required field.
  • The token response says what was granted. Section 7 requires the server to return the authorization_details "as granted by the resource owner and assigned to the respective access token". They may differ from what was asked (section 7.1), and a note in section 3 says the user may grant a subset. This lesson's advice is that the client compares the two.
  • The resource server is told. Section 9 requires the authorization server to make the data available to the resource server. For a JWT access token it recommends a top-level claim (9.1). In an introspection response, if included, it must be the top-level member authorization_details (9.2).
  • Scope still works alongside. If both are present the server must process them together and must show the user the merged set (section 3.1).

What the resource server must still do. Everything. Section 1 of the RFC says the authorization server and the resource server "will together enforce this consent". The object in the token is data. If the payments API checks that a payment_initiation object is present and does not compare its fields with the payment in front of it, the token is as broad as the scope was. Check 44 of the lab is that API. How to compare is the API's own definition: section 6.1 says "there is no standardized mechanism to compare two arbitrary authorization detail requests".

The specification's own security considerations (section 12): the parameter travels through the user agent, so the user can modify it, and "clients MUST protect authorization_details against tampering and swapping" where integrity is a concern, with a signed request object or with PAR. String comparisons follow RFC 8259 with no further normalization. The server must sanitize the data to prevent injection. Section 13 adds that personal data in the details must be kept from leaking, for example through referrer headers. In a payment both concerns are real. Section 3 says implementers may consider PAR for exactly this, and Part C of the lab pushes every request that carries details.

Two connections. Module 23, Agent authority and approvals, teaches that an approval must bind the exact parameters that will execute. authorization_details is where OAuth carries those parameters from the consent screen to the API. And RAR does not replace server-side authorization: it narrows what a token may do, and the API still decides whose objects the caller may touch, which is module 9, Object-level authorization.

Step-up authentication

Step-up authentication lets a resource server refuse one request because of how, or how long ago, the user authenticated. RFC 9470 defines it in four moves:

  1. The resource server reads two facts about the token: auth_time, when the user authenticated, and acr, an authentication context class reference that names how. They come from the claims of a JWT access token (section 6.1) or from the introspection response (section 6.2). Section 6.1 notes that the values "will not change in the event of access token renewals": a refreshed token is not a fresher authentication.
  2. If they do not meet its policy, it challenges. The error code is insufficient_user_authentication. Two parameters say what would be enough: acr_values, a space-separated list in order of preference, and max_age, the allowed number of seconds since the last active authentication. Both may appear in one challenge (section 3).
  3. The client starts a new authorization request carrying those values as the acr_values and max_age request parameters that OpenID Connect Core section 3.1.2.1 defines (section 4, which says the client should do this). The client does not look inside the access token to decide: section 2 says "a client must not attempt to inspect the content of the access token".
  4. The authorization server authenticates the user again and issues a new token whose acr and auth_time reflect it. Section 5 says the server should treat the requested acr as necessary: if it cannot be met, the request fails with unmet_authentication_requirements. That stops a client looping on tokens the API has already refused.

An acr value is only a string. OpenID Connect Core section 2 says: "Parties using this claim will need to agree upon the meanings of the values used". The resource server trusts the authorization server's statement that a second factor was used. RFC 9470 section 9 adds two cautions. The challenge can tell an attacker which users or resources are treated as high value. And a resource server may send the challenge without first validating the token, but doing so leaks its requirements to a caller who has not shown it can obtain a token. The lab validates first.

This is not the step-up in module 20. Module 20, MCP server authorization teaches the MCP specification's "Step-Up Authorization Flow". The words are similar and the thing is different:

QuestionScope step-up (module 20)Authentication step-up (this module)
What is missingPermission. The token does not cover the operationAssurance. The token covers the operation, but the user's authentication is too old or too weak
Error codeinsufficient_scope, RFC 6750 section 3.1insufficient_user_authentication, RFC 9470 section 3
StatusRFC 6750 says the server should answer 403The examples in RFC 9470 use 401
What the challenge carriesscopeacr_values, max_age, or both
What the client asks for nextMore scope. In MCP, the union of what it had and what was challengedThe same access, with a stronger or fresher authentication
What the user doesConsents to moreSigns in again

One response can carry both. RFC 9470 section 3 allows the resource server to add the scope attribute to an authentication challenge when the request is also lacking scope. Checks 52 and 59 of the lab are the two errors side by side.

Legacy flows a reviewer will meet

Module 4 gives these one table row. Here is the fuller account, because both still appear in designs and in server defaults.

QuestionImplicit grantResource owner password credentials grant
What it doesThe authorization endpoint returns the access token itself, in the URI fragment of the redirect, with no code and no token request (RFC 6749 section 4.2)The client collects the user's username and password and posts them to the token endpoint (RFC 6749 section 4.3)
What goes wrongThe token is in a URL, so it can leak, be replayed and be injected, and there is no standardized way to sender-constrain a token issued this way (RFC 9700 section 2.1.2). There is no client authentication (RFC 6749 section 4.2)The client sees the password. RFC 9700 section 2.4 says the grant "insecurely exposes the credentials of the resource owner to the client", trains users to enter credentials outside the authorization server, and is not designed to work with two-factor authentication
What RFC 9700 says, exactly"clients SHOULD NOT use the implicit grant (response type token) or other response types issuing access tokens in the authorization response, unless access token injection in the authorization response is prevented and the aforementioned token leakage vectors are mitigated" (section 2.1.2). A recommendation, with a conditionIt "MUST NOT be used" (section 2.4). A requirement, with no condition
The OAuth 2.1 Internet-Draft, revision 16Omits it. Section 10.1 of the draft says response_type=token "is no longer defined in OAuth 2.1". This is a draft, not a standardOmits it (section 10 of the draft)
How to recognize it in a designresponse_type=token in an authorization URL. #access_token= in a redirect. implicit in a client's grant_types or token in its response_types (RFC 7591 section 2). Server metadata with no grant_types_supported: RFC 8414 section 2 says the default, if omitted, includes implicitThe app has its own sign-in form for the bank's credentials. grant_type=password with username and password at the token endpoint. password in a client's grant_types. A note that a second factor cannot be used with this client

RFC 6749 itself warned about the password grant in section 10.7: it "maintains the password anti-pattern this protocol seeks to avoid". The draft says its removal of response_type=token does not affect other response types that return something else from the authorization endpoint. Those belong to OpenID Connect, the subject of module 35, OpenID Connect and ID tokens.

FAPI 2.0: one published composition

The FAPI 2.0 Security Profile is an OpenID Foundation Final Specification (22 February 2025). It selects from the controls above and from modules 4 and 7, and makes them mandatory together. Its keywords are "shall", "should" and "may".

The attacker model, as far as this lesson can state it. The profile says it "has been proved by formal analysis to meet the stated attacker model" (section 1), and that it aims to follow the recommendations in RFC 9700 (section 5.1.1). The attacker model is a separate document, the FAPI 2.0 Attacker Model, which this lesson has not read, so it is not summarized here. What this lesson can report is a different list, the attacker model of RFC 9700 itself (section 3). It is not the FAPI one. It describes five kinds of attacker: a web attacker who runs their own clients, servers and pages (A1), a network attacker who controls the network outside what cryptography such as TLS protects (A2), and attackers who can read the authorization response (A3), read the authorization request (A4), or acquire an access token (A5). The profile's own security considerations mention an attacker who can intercept an authorization request and one who can obtain DPoP proofs, and call them A3 and A5 in its own model's numbering (sections 6.4 and 6.2). In RFC 9700 the attacker who reads the authorization request is A4, not A3, so the two lists number their attackers differently. Do not carry one over to the other. The profile also says what it leaves out: only confidential clients are in scope, because the working group "is not currently aware of any mechanisms that would allow public clients to be secured to the same degree" (section 5.1.1).

ControlWhat the profile requires (section)The attack it answers
Client authenticationAuthorization servers shall authenticate clients with mutual TLS (RFC 8705 section 2) or private_key_jwt, shall support only confidential clients, and shall accept only their issuer identifier, as a string, in the assertion's aud. Clients send it that way (5.3.2.1, 5.3.3.1)A leaked or stored shared secret. An assertion reused at another server

Clients shall send only client_id and request_uri to the authorization endpoint (5.3.2.2, 5.3.3.2)Reading or editing the request in the browser

Issuer identificationServers shall return the iss parameter of RFC 9207 in the authorization response, and clients shall check it (5.3.2.2, 5.3.3.2)A mix-up attack on a client that uses more than one authorization server
Sender-constrained tokensServers shall issue only sender-constrained access tokens, by mutual TLS or DPoP. Resource servers shall support and verify them (5.3.2.1, 5.3.4)A stolen access token (module 7)
Legacy grantsServers shall reject the resource owner password credentials grant (5.3.2.1). With response_type fixed to code, there is no implicit grantPasswords handed to clients. Tokens in URLs
Resource serverShall accept tokens in the HTTP header and not in query parameters, shall verify "the validity, integrity, expiration and revocation status" of tokens, and shall verify that the authorization the token represents is sufficient for the request (5.3.4)Tokens in URLs and logs. Revoked or under-privileged tokens
Transport and cryptographyTLS 1.2 or later on every endpoint (5.2.1). JWTs use PS256, ES256 or EdDSA with Ed25519, and never none. RSA keys are at least 2048 bits. Credentials not handled by users have at least 128 bits of entropy (5.4.1)Network attackers. Weak keys and guessable values
Redirects and metadataNo open redirectors at the server or the client. No http redirect URIs except loopback for native clients. Clients shall take the server's endpoints only from its metadata document and check that the issuer in it matches (5.3.2.1, 5.3.2.2, 5.3.3.1)Leaked authorization responses. A client configured with an attacker's endpoint

Three things about that list. First, the profile does not require RAR. A note in section 5.3.2.2 recommends it "when the scope parameter is not expressive enough". It does not mention RFC 9470 at all. A deployment can meet the profile with a coarse scope and no step-up, so Part E of the lab adds both on its own account. Second, a few requirements cut against habit: the server shall not use refresh token rotation except in extraordinary circumstances (5.3.2.1). Its note gives the reason: rotation brings no security benefit with confidential clients and sender-constrained tokens, and it causes operational problems. Third, the profile says what it does not solve. Section 6.5 describes a browser-swapping attack and says "there is no way to completely prevent this attack if the authorization response leaks to an attacker in any redirect-based protocol". Section 6.2 notes that DPoP does not sign the request body. Section 5.1.2 forbids a derived profile from removing mandatory behaviors, because doing so "is likely to invalidate the formal security analysis".

The teaching point. High assurance is a composition: each control answers one named attack by one kind of attacker, and the list is only as good as the attacker model behind it. An API can have every control above in place and still return another customer's payment to a correctly authenticated caller. The profile has one clause that touches this: the resource server shall verify that the authorization the token represents is sufficient for the requested resource access (5.3.4). It does not say how, and no other control in the list looks at which object was asked for. Deciding whose object it is stays the API's own code. That is module 9, and it is check 70 of the lab.

sections.heading: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.heading_text: 5. What it proves, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
Proves, control by control: private_key_jwt proves the caller can use the private key that matches the public key registered for this client, for this server, within the assertion's short lifetime, and once if the server tracks jti. PAR proves the parameters the server acted on are the ones an authenticated client sent it directly. authorization_details on a token prove which specific access the authorization server recorded as granted. acr and auth_time are the authorization server's statement of how and when the user authenticated. A deployment that meets FAPI 2.0 has all of the controls in the table in section 3, analyzed together against a stated attacker.

Doesn't prove who may do what to which object. Every control here is about the client, the request, the token or the user's authentication. None of them looks at whether the object named in the API call belongs to the caller. That decision is made in the API, per object and per operation (modules 9 and 10, Property and function authorization).

Doesn't prove the user understood what they approved. RAR makes the consent screen able to show the real payee and amount. It cannot make anyone read it. In check 21 of the lab the user is shown a request that was edited in the browser, and approves it. FAPI 2.0 section 7 lists "Insufficient understanding of the end-user granting access to data" among its privacy threats. Module 23 covers the same limit for agent approvals.

Doesn't prove anything about where the client keeps its private key. Asymmetric client authentication moves the target from the server's table to the client's key. If that key sits in a repository or an environment variable, anyone who reads it is the client, with a credential that looks stronger on paper. Who owns that key, when it rotates and how it is withdrawn is module 8.

Doesn't make a token single use. Nothing in RFC 9396 limits how many times a token may be used. Measured on a call the lab does not make: the token from check 38 pays 45.00 EUR to ExampleAir a second time and gets 201 again. One approved payment being executed once is a rule for the API to enforce, and it is module 11, Business flows and idempotency.

Step-up is not sign-in. RFC 9470 section 9 says: "This document MUST NOT be used to position OAuth as an authentication protocol." The resource server learns how the authorization server authenticated the user. The client learns nothing about who the user is, and must not treat the new access token as a login. Module 4 makes the same point about access tokens in general.

sections.heading: 6. Prove it
sections.html:
A working deployment must refuse every one of these. If any is accepted, the control it belongs to is broken:

  • A client registered for private_key_jwt presenting a client secret, or presenting two methods in one request.
  • An assertion signed with any key other than the registered one, or with an algorithm other than the registered one, including an HMAC keyed with the client's public key.
  • An assertion whose aud names another server. If your policy is issuer-only, one whose aud is the token endpoint URL.
  • An assertion presented at or after its exp, one whose exp is further away than your cap, and the same assertion presented twice.
  • With PAR required: an authorization request that carries its parameters on the URL.
  • A request_uri used a second time, used after expires_in, made up, or presented with a different client_id. After the last of these, the rightful client can still use it.
  • A pushed request with no client authentication, and one that itself contains a request_uri.
  • Parameters added to the authorization URL next to a request_uri: they must have no effect.
  • An authorization_details object with an unknown type, an unknown field or a missing field, and a known type the client is not registered to use.
  • At the API: a payment whose payee, amount or currency differs from the granted object in any way.
  • At the API: a consequential request with a token whose auth_time is older than the policy or whose acr is weaker. The refusal names insufficient_user_authentication and says what is required. An invalid token on the same endpoint gets invalid_token and no policy.
  • response_type=token, grant_type=password and code_challenge_method=plain.
  • In the client: an authorization response whose iss is not the issuer the request was sent to.
  • A bound token presented without the key it is bound to.
  • And, with every one of the above in place: a request for an object that belongs to another customer.
